channel.title: horowitz.law: Georgia Appellate Watch
channel.description: AI-assisted synopses of new Georgia appellate, Eleventh Circuit, and U.S. Supreme Court opinions, filtered for civil litigation and insurance practice. Each synopsis is AI-drafted; the linked opinion is the authority. A curated core, not a complete docket. This feed covers the most recent two years; older opinions are archived by year at https://horowitz.law/archive.

item.title: Douglas v. Bhakta (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: In an auto-accident suit, defendant admitted in his answer that he was a Kansas resident at the time of the accident and at the time of suit but did not assert insufficiency of service of process by motion filed before or simultaneously with the answer. The Court of Appeals held that a defendant waives the defense of insufficiency of service of process under OCGA section 9-11-12(h)(1)(B) by failing to raise it in the original answer or a contemporaneously filed motion, and that a general reference to lack of personal jurisdiction does not preserve the service defense. The court further held that, because defendant admitted out-of-state residency in his answer, he was subject to service under the Nonresident Motorist Act, and his later conclusory affidavit asserting Georgia residency could not overcome that binding judicial admission, which he never moved to withdraw. The court also clarified that a nonresident defendant involved in a Georgia accident is subject to jurisdiction under the NRMA when nonresident at both the time of accident and time of suit, while the Long Arm Statute applies when the defendant was a Georgia resident at the time of the accident and later became a nonresident. The dismissal was reversed. Why it matters: It clarifies that the service-of-process defense in NRMA auto cases must be raised in the original answer or a simultaneously filed motion or it is waived, and that an answer admission of residency is a binding judicial admission that a later self-serving affidavit cannot overcome absent a motion to withdraw. Also: The trial court had granted defendant's motion to withdraw deemed admissions under OCGA section 9-11-36(b), including admissions concerning residence. Following its holding in Division 1, the Court of Appeals reversed the withdrawal as to the residency-related requests because defendant had admitted Kansas residency and failed to preserve the service defense, but found no abuse of discretion as to the remaining requests and directed that discovery be reopened on remand in light of newly provided eyewitness evidence. Why it matters: It illustrates that withdrawal of deemed admissions under OCGA section 9-11-36(b) cannot be used to undo a binding pleading admission that controls a dispositive jurisdictional issue. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10878114/jovan-douglas-v-chirag-bhakta/

item.title: Yamaha Motor Manufacturing Corporation of America v. Hall (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: In a products-liability action arising from a golf cart rollover, the trial court excluded the specific contents of the manufacturer's warning labels and operator's manual, allowing only evidence that warnings existed and how they were delivered. The Court of Appeals held that the contents of the warnings were relevant and admissible to the risk-utility analysis on the design-defect claim under the Banks 'efficacy of warnings' factor, even though those contents were inadmissible on the communication-based failure-to-warn claim because the operator never read them. The court reasoned that evidence inadmissible for one purpose may be admissible for another and that the error was not harmless, and it rejected the contention that the manufacturer waived the argument by not using the phrase 'risk-utility analysis' below. Why it matters: It clarifies that the contents of a manufacturer's warnings are admissible on the design-defect risk-utility analysis under Banks even when those contents are inadmissible on a failure-to-warn claim, and confirms that no magic words are required to preserve a relevance argument. Also: The manufacturer argued for the first time on appeal that it owed no duty to ensure its warning labels and operator's manual remained with the golf cart through the product's life cycle. The court held the argument was not preserved because, under OCGA section 9-11-50 (a), a directed-verdict motion must state its specific grounds, and the manufacturer never raised the absence of a duty when it moved for a directed verdict below, having instead argued only the adequacy of communication and proximate cause. Why it matters: It reinforces that a ground for directed verdict not specifically stated in the trial court motion cannot be raised for the first time on appeal. Also: The manufacturer invited the court to revisit AU Medical Center v. Dale, in which a plurality held that the term 'brought' in the former version of OCGA section 51-12-33 (b) refers to the number of named defendants remaining at the time of trial, which had led the trial court to enter the full judgment against the manufacturer despite the jury allocating fault to dismissed non-parties. The court declined the invitation to revisit that holding. Why it matters: It signals that the court will not reconsider its apportionment construction in AU Medical Center v. Dale regarding allocation of fault to dismissed non-parties under the former statute. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10878111/yamaha-motor-manufacturing-coporation-of-america-v-elizabeth-hall/

item.title: T. M. v. University of Maryland Medical System Corporation (U.S.)
item.category: Supreme Court of the United States
item.description: The Supreme Court held that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal district court jurisdiction over cases brought by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments rendered before the federal proceedings commenced and seeking district court review and rejection of those judgments, regardless of whether the state-court judgment remains subject to further review in state appellate proceedings. The Court rejected the argument that the doctrine applies only to final judgments rendered by the highest court of a State, reasoning that the doctrine rests on the functional distinction between original and appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. sections 1331 and 1257, not solely on a negative inference from section 1257. Petitioner had sued in federal court to declare a state consent order unconstitutional and unenforceable while simultaneously appealing it in state court. The Court resolved a conflict among the Courts of Appeals. Why it matters: The decision clarifies the scope of a threshold jurisdictional doctrine and confirms that Rooker-Feldman can bar a federal suit even when the underlying state-court judgment is still on appeal, which directly affects civil litigants pursuing parallel state and federal proceedings. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10877643/t-m-v-university-of-md-medical-system-corporation-revisions-61926/

item.title: Lloyd v. City of Atlanta (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: Plaintiff, injured when his bike tire became lodged in a city storm drain grate, sent an ante litem notice jointly addressed to the City of Atlanta and Fulton County demanding a "global settlement amount" of $2,000,000. The Court of Appeals held that this notice failed to comply with OCGA section 36-33-5(e), which requires a specific amount of monetary damages being sought from the municipal corporation, because demanding a single global amount from two entities jointly does not identify the specific amount sought from the city alone and leaves the city to speculate what portion constituted an offer it could accept. The court noted it need not decide whether subsection (e) requires strict or substantial compliance because the notice failed under either standard, and rejected the argument that use of "and/or" cured the defect, finding the term was used only to reference the applicable notice statutes. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that an ante litem notice presenting a single combined settlement demand against a municipality and another governmental entity, without specifying the amount sought from the municipality alone, fails the specific-amount requirement of OCGA section 36-33-5(e) and bars suit as a condition precedent. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10875860/maugan-lloyd-v-city-of-atlanta/

item.title: Cayamcela v. Advocacy Trust, LLC (Ga.)
item.description: In a medical malpractice and wrongful death action arising from a patient's death in the ICU after childbirth, the jury returned a $42 million verdict against a doctor and a medical staffing agency. The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the trial court's exclusion under OCGA section 24-7-702(b) of a defense expert's testimony about ICU care, holding the court acted within its gatekeeping discretion where the expert repeatedly admitted he had not reviewed the relevant ICU records well enough to opine on that care and that the matter fell outside his specialty. The court rejected the argument that these gaps went only to credibility rather than admissibility. Why it matters: The decision confirms that a trial court may exclude expert testimony as unreliable under Rule 702(b) when the expert concedes an insufficient factual basis, and that such deficiencies bear on admissibility, not merely weight. Also: The court held that the noneconomic damages cap of OCGA section 51-13-1(b) could not be constitutionally applied to the jury's verdict. Relying on its companion decision in Clark v. Leigh, issued the same day, the court reaffirmed that stare decisis preserves Nestlehutt and that where any part of a medical malpractice award is for noneconomic damages subject to the right to a jury trial, the cap cannot be applied without violating that right. Why it matters: The ruling confirms that the medical malpractice noneconomic damages cap remains unenforceable as applied to jury verdicts that include noneconomic damages, leaving Nestlehutt intact and extending its reasoning to wrongful death awards. Also: The court held that the defendants affirmatively waived their challenge to a jury instruction stating that defendants bore the burden of proof on whether other medical professionals were the sole proximate cause. By proposing the opposite instruction, then withdrawing all proposed instructions, and stating multiple times that they had no objection to the court's charge, the defendants waived even substantial-error review under OCGA section 5-5-24(c). Why it matters: The decision clarifies that affirmative waiver, by withdrawing requested instructions and acquiescing in the charge given, forecloses substantial-error review of an instructional error on appeal. Also: The court affirmed the roughly $11.8 million attorney fee award under OCGA section 9-11-68, holding the plaintiffs' settlement offer satisfied subsection (a)(7) because it stated plaintiffs would pay their own fees and expenses, which were incurred for the claims rather than part of them. The court further held that OCGA section 9-15-16 and Couch bar use of a contingency fee agreement to prove the reasonableness of fees but do not bar considering the agreement for other purposes, such as proving total fees incurred, and that the trial court properly established reasonableness through other evidence. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that a contingency fee agreement may be used to establish total fees incurred even though it cannot prove their reasonableness under OCGA section 9-15-16, and addresses what satisfies the offer requirements of OCGA section 9-11-68(a)(7). AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10875605/cayamcela-v-advocacy-trust-llc-two-cases/

item.title: Clark v. Leigh (Ga.)
item.description: In a medical malpractice and wrongful death action where a jury awarded $29,250,000 for the full value of the decedent's life, $2,500,000 for pain and suffering, and medical expenses, the trial court applied the OCGA section 51-13-1(b) noneconomic damages cap to reduce the wrongful death award to $350,000. The Supreme Court of Georgia reaffirmed Nestlehutt, holding that the right to trial by jury under the Georgia Constitution does not permit applying the cap to pain and suffering and loss of consortium damages in medical malpractice actions, and declined to overrule it under stare decisis. The court then held that, under ordinary principles of statutory construction and in light of Nestlehutt, the cap statute cannot operate at all on a judgment in a case like this one, where the jury's verdict includes noneconomic damages for a cause of action to which the jury trial right applies, because making it operative would require impermissibly rewriting the statute. The court vacated the order applying the cap and remanded for the trial court to decide the defendants' excessiveness claim as to the wrongful death award. Why it matters: The decision reaffirms that the OCGA section 51-13-1(b) medical malpractice noneconomic damages cap is unenforceable as to constitutionally protected jury-determined damages and extends that result, on statutory-construction grounds, to render the cap inoperative on the entire judgment including 'full value of life' wrongful death damages in such cases. Also: The plaintiffs argued the defendants waived the right to assert the statutory damages cap by failing to raise it in the pretrial order. The court held the trial court did not abuse its discretion in allowing the defendants to raise the cap for the first time in their post-trial motions, reasoning that the cap statute is not an affirmative defense but a statutory limit on the amount of recoverable damages that is triggered only once a verdict exceeds the threshold. Why it matters: It clarifies that a statutory damages cap need not be raised in the pretrial order or at trial and may be asserted for the first time in a timely post-trial motion. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10875604/clark-v-leigh-and-vice-versa/

item.title: Crook v. Six Flags Over Georgia II, L.P. (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: Plaintiff, the surviving spouse and administrator of an employee who died after falling from a cargo van at a theme park, sued the employer and a co-worker, and the trial court dismissed under OCGA 9-11-12(b)(1) for lack of subject matter jurisdiction based on the exclusive remedy provision of the Workers' Compensation Act. The Court of Appeals held that the Act's exclusivity bar is a statutory affirmative defense, not a question of subject matter jurisdiction, so the employer bears the burden of proving the bar applies and the defense can be waived if not timely raised. The court disapproved Kellogg Co. v. Pinkston, Savannah Hospitality Servs. v. Scriven, and T & R S. Sanitation v. Lowe to the extent they treated the exclusivity bar as jurisdictional. The trial court therefore erred in placing the burden on plaintiff to disprove the bar. Why it matters: This decision establishes that the Workers' Compensation Act exclusive remedy provision must be litigated as a waivable affirmative defense, with the burden on the employer, rather than as a non-waivable subject matter jurisdiction bar, which changes how WCA exclusivity is raised and proved in Georgia tort and wrongful death cases. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10875034/lokin-crook-v-six-flags-over-georgia-ii-lp/

item.title: Allied Property & Casualty Insurance Company v. Bloodworth Wholesale Drugs Inc. (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: Two pharmacies sued for their alleged role in the opioid epidemic sought defense and indemnity under liability and druggist liability policies covering damages 'because of bodily injury.' The insurers contended that the underlying government and healthcare suits seek economic losses not tied to identifiable injured persons and are therefore not covered, and the district courts granted summary judgment for the insurers. The Eleventh Circuit found no clear controlling Georgia or Florida precedent on whether such opioid lawsuits seek damages 'because of bodily injury,' distinguishing Georgia decisions like Cesnik, Lunceford, Presidential Hotel, and O'Dell as not dispositive. It certified to the Supreme Court of Georgia and the Supreme Court of Florida the question whether the policies require the insurers to defend and indemnify the insureds in the underlying opioid litigation. Why it matters: The certification flags an unresolved, high-value coverage question of whether CGL and druggist liability policies covering 'damages because of bodily injury' reach opioid-epidemic suits seeking economic losses, leaving Georgia coverage law on the point to be settled by the Supreme Court of Georgia. Unpublished; not binding precedent. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10873765/allied-property-casualty-insurance-company-v-bloodworth-wholesale-drugs/

item.title: Waddle Trucking of Mississippi, Inc. v. Johnson (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: A trucking defendant in a personal injury action was served in state court, after which a codefendant removed the case to federal court, where the defendant filed an answer that was untimely under Fed.R.Civ.P. 81(c)(2). After remand, the state court entered default judgment against the defendant. The Court of Appeals held that the answer filed in district court, even though untimely there, prevented default in state court because the district court never struck the answer and no default was entered under Fed.R.Civ.P. 55, and because on remand the defendant still had time remaining to answer. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that an answer filed in federal court after removal continues to have effect on remand and prevents entry of default in state court so long as the federal court did not strike it or enter default, even if the federal answer was untimely. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10873711/waddle-trucking-of-mississippi-inc-v-aileen-johnson/

item.title: Keathley v. Buddy Ayers Construction, Inc. (U.S.)
item.category: Supreme Court of the United States
item.description: A debtor in an open Chapter 13 bankruptcy failed to disclose a personal-injury claim arising from a car accident, and the lower courts applied judicial estoppel to bar the tort suit using the Fifth Circuit's two-factor test, asking only whether the debtor knew the underlying facts and had a potential motive to conceal. The Supreme Court, assuming without deciding that judicial estoppel can apply in the bankruptcy context and that inadvertence or mistake can be an exception, held that courts must look to the totality of the circumstances surrounding the omission. The Court found the Fifth Circuit's approach both too rigid, because equity eschews mechanical rules, and too broad, because its motive criterion is almost always satisfied, making it a poor fit for assessing whether an omission was actually inadvertent or mistaken. Why it matters: It establishes that whether a plaintiff-debtor's failure to schedule a personal-injury claim was inadvertent or mistaken for judicial-estoppel purposes turns on the totality of the circumstances rather than a knowledge-plus-motive test, governing how civil litigants raise and defend against judicial estoppel when a tort claim was omitted from bankruptcy schedules. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10873663/keathley-v-buddy-ayers-construction-inc/

item.title: Hodge v. Molson Coors Beverage Company USA, LLC (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: A family injured by a semitruck sued a freight broker and a shipper, alleging negligent hiring of the carrier. The district court held that the FAAAA preempted the negligent-selection claim against the broker. Following the Supreme Court's decision in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, which abrogated the Eleventh Circuit's prior holding in Aspen American Insurance Co. v. Landstar Ranger, the court vacated and remanded, noting the district court had relied on now-abrogated caselaw. Why it matters: It applies the Supreme Court's recent holding that the FAAAA does not preempt negligent-selection-of-carrier claims against brokers, abrogating prior Eleventh Circuit precedent that had foreclosed such claims. Also: The court affirmed dismissal of the negligent-hiring claim against the shipper, applying Maryland law, which requires that the defendant's failure to undertake reasonable inquiry resulted in the contractor's hiring and that the hiring proximately caused the plaintiff's injury. The shipper hired Schneider, who hired Coyote, who hired the carrier, leaving the shipper three steps removed from hiring the operator. Because plaintiffs neither identified authority extending the theory that far nor alleged that the selection of Schneider was negligent, the claim failed, and influence over the hiring process was held not equivalent to actually hiring the carrier. Why it matters: It clarifies that negligent-hiring liability under Maryland law does not extend to a party several contractual layers removed from the entity that hired the operator absent an allegation tying the harm to the directly hired contractor. Unpublished; not binding precedent. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10873661/willy-hodge-v-molson-coors-beverage-company-usa-llc/

item.title: Ya Mon Expeditions, LLC v. YATCO, LLC (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: In an interlocutory appeal from the denial of a motion to compel arbitration under the FAA, an MLS company sought to compel nonsignatory yacht-seller plaintiffs to arbitrate antitrust claims based on a subscription agreement their brokers allegedly accepted. The court held that under Florida law, which governs the threshold question of whether an arbitration agreement exists, the party seeking to compel arbitration bears the burden of proving an enforceable agreement, and the movant relied on speculation and assumption rather than evidence that the brokers actually listed the plaintiffs' yachts on its website or accepted the relevant version of the agreement. The court rejected the movant's argument that the nonsignatory plaintiffs opposing arbitration bore the burden of disproving its evidence. Why it matters: It clarifies that the FAA presumption favoring arbitration does not apply to the threshold question of whether an agreement to arbitrate exists, and that state law places the burden of proving an enforceable arbitration agreement on the party seeking to compel it. Also: The court held that the nonsignatory plaintiffs could not be bound to arbitrate under an agency-ratification theory. Applying the Florida Supreme Court's full-knowledge requirement, the court held that a principal ratifies an agent's pre-agency acceptance of a contract only on a showing that the principal had full knowledge of the agreement and its terms, and constructive knowledge does not suffice. Because the movant submitted no evidence that the plaintiffs knew of the agreement or its terms, and the brokers' knowledge could not be imputed because it was acquired before any agency relationship formed, ratification did not apply. Why it matters: It establishes that under controlling Florida Supreme Court precedent a nonsignatory principal cannot ratify an agent's pre-agency acceptance of an arbitration agreement absent full actual knowledge of the agreement and its terms. Also: The court held that equitable estoppel did not bind the nonsignatory plaintiffs to arbitrate. A signatory may enforce an arbitration clause against a nonsignatory under equitable estoppel only if the nonsignatory relies on the agreement to assert its claims and the dispute falls within the clause. Because the plaintiffs' federal antitrust claims arose from statutory duties unrelated to the subscription agreement and did not require reference to or construction of that agreement, the plaintiffs were not claiming the benefits of the contract while avoiding its burdens. Why it matters: It clarifies that equitable estoppel cannot compel a nonsignatory to arbitrate where the asserted claims rest on independent statutory duties and do not depend on the contract containing the arbitration clause. Unpublished; not binding precedent. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10872980/ya-mon-expeditions-llc-v-yatco-llc/

item.title: Vu v. City of Atlanta (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: A city employee driving a city-owned truck rear-ended plaintiff's car, and plaintiff served a municipal ante litem notice demanding $1,000,000. The trial court dismissed the suit, accepting the city's argument that the notice failed to state a 'specific amount' under OCGA § 36-33-5(e) because it exceeded the $500,000 sovereign-immunity waiver for negligent motor-vehicle use. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that OCGA § 36-92-2 does not cap or limit the waiver but automatically waives immunity up to $500,000 while specifying ways to increase it, and reaffirming that the demanded amount need not be one the municipality is capable of accepting. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that a municipal ante litem notice satisfies the specific-amount requirement of OCGA § 36-33-5(e) even when the demand exceeds the automatic sovereign-immunity waiver under OCGA § 36-92-2. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10872456/jenny-vu-v-city-of-atlanta/

item.title: GoAuto Insurance Company v. 2B Claims Services Inc. (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: An insurer sued the third-party claims adjuster it hired, alleging the adjuster negligently failed to advise it about the risk of excess bad-faith liability after the insurer let a checks-in-hand policy-limits deadline pass and later settled for about $220,000 above the policy limits. Applying Florida bad-faith law, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the adjuster, holding that a claims adjuster has no duty to advise an insurer about its own legal risk of excess bad-faith exposure because such advice constitutes legal advice, and that the insurer's own decision to demand signed releases and not deliver the checks by the deadline, not the adjuster's conduct, proximately caused the excess settlement. The court noted the insurer knew of the checks-in-hand requirement eleven days before the deadline and could have delivered the checks. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that a third-party claims adjuster owes no duty to advise an insurer about its own extracontractual bad-faith exposure and that an insurer's independent settlement and payment decisions, not the adjuster's handling, control causation in a negligence claim against the adjuster. Unpublished; not binding precedent. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10872097/goauto-insurance-company-v-2b-claims-services-inc/

item.title: State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. & GEICO Indemnity Co. v. Barnor-Cooper (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: The Court of Appeals reversed the denial of summary judgment to State Farm and GEICO in a UM claim arising from a hit-and-run collision, holding the plaintiff was not entitled to UM benefits under either policy. Injured while making a delivery in a Turo-rented Buick, she was not an insured under the State Farm policy: the Buick was not a "temporary substitute car" because the scheduled vehicle it would have replaced had been sold, and the named-insured LLC is a separate legal entity from its members and managers. Why it matters: Reads the 'temporary substitute car' and named-insured provisions strictly: a borrowed vehicle is not a temporary substitute once the scheduled car it would replace has been sold, and an LLC policyholder is a separate legal entity from its members and managers, which narrows who qualifies as an insured for UM purposes. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10862301/state-farm-mutual-automobile-insurance-company-v-charity-barnor-cooper/

item.title: Johnson v. Everett (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: In a medical-malpractice case that ended in a defense verdict, the Court of Appeals held that the trial court mistakenly believed it had no choice but to let the jury consider the emergency-medical-care gross-negligence standard of O.C.G.A. § 51-1-29.5, an issue the parties had not listed in their pretrial order, when in fact the court had discretion to disallow it. The court vacated the denial of a new trial and remanded for the court to exercise that discretion, and found no error in admitting the defense expert's opinions or a complaint from another case. Why it matters: A pretrial order frames the issues for trial, but the court keeps discretion over an issue the parties left out of it, and treating that discretion as nonexistent is reversible error. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10862062/john-johnson-v-christopher-b-everett/

item.title: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC (U.S.)
item.category: Supreme Court of the United States
item.description: An injured motorist sued a transportation broker for negligent hiring, alleging that the broker selected a motor carrier with a subpar federal safety rating that was reasonably likely to cause crashes. The Court held that even assuming the FAAAA's preemption provision in 49 U.S.C. section 14501(c)(1) would otherwise reach the negligent-hiring claim, the safety exception in section 14501(c)(2)(A) saves it because such a claim is one regulating safety 'with respect to motor vehicles.' Construing 'with respect to' to mean 'concerns' or 'regards,' the Court reasoned that requiring a broker to exercise ordinary care in selecting a carrier concerns the trucks that will transport the goods. Why it matters: The decision resolves a circuit split and establishes that state-law negligent-hiring claims against freight brokers who select unsafe motor carriers are not preempted by the FAAAA, abrogating the contrary Eleventh Circuit rule that had governed in Georgia. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10858760/montgomery-v-caribe-transport-ii-llc/

item.title: Loveless v. GSH Investments, LLC (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: The Court of Appeals reversed summary judgment for an apartment owner whose tenant's visitor was injured when an exterior wooden staircase collapsed, and affirmed the denial of the plaintiff's motions to compel. Before buying the complex the owner received an appraisal and an insurer survey flagging below-average condition and deferred maintenance, yet it never inspected the building exteriors or the stairways and kept no formal inspection process, relying on tenants to report problems. That evidence created a jury question on whether the owner had constructive knowledge of the hazard. Why it matters: Prior reports flagging below-average condition, combined with the owner's lack of any inspection routine, can supply constructive knowledge of a hazard and create a jury question that defeats summary judgment. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10815924/monnie-loveless-v-gsh-investments-llc/

item.title: Cannon v. Safeco Insurance Co. of Illinois (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: The Court of Appeals reversed the dismissal of a failure-to-settle action against a liability insurer. After a $1.65 million excess judgment was entered against its insured following a fatal collision, the insured alleged that Safeco had interpleaded and tendered its $100,000 limits into the court registry without obtaining any release of the claims against him. Because an insurer must give equal consideration to the insured's interests and may be liable for an excess judgment for a negligent or bad-faith failure to settle, the complaint stated a claim. Why it matters: Tendering policy limits by interpleader, without obtaining a release for the insured, does not by itself discharge the insurer or bar a later failure-to-settle or bad-faith claim. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10809283/trever-cannon-v-safeco-insurance-company-of-illinois/

item.title: Sullivan v. Trustgard Insurance Co. (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: The Court of Appeals reversed partial summary judgment that had set uninsured-motorist limits at $100,000 on a commercial auto policy. The insurer's application directed that its uninsured-motorist selection section was not to be used in Georgia and required a state-specific supplement, and neither that section nor the mandatory offer form was signed or initialed. Because the insurer never obtained a valid written election of reduced limits, the court held the coverage defaulted to the $1 million liability limit. Why it matters: Without a compliant, signed election of reduced uninsured-motorist limits, the coverage defaults to the bodily-injury liability limit under O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10809157/stephen-michael-sullivan-v-trustgard-insurance-company/

item.title: Radheshvar, LLC v. Perez Larios (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: The Court of Appeals affirmed the denial of summary judgment to a motel owner in a premises case brought by a guest's social visitor who was attacked in a breezeway. The owner argued the visitor was a licensee owed only a duty to avoid wilful or wanton injury, but the court held a jury could find he was an invitee, leaving the applicable standard of care for the factfinder. Why it matters: Invitee-versus-licensee status under O.C.G.A. §§ 51-3-1 and 51-3-2 is often a jury question, which can leave the standard of care for the factfinder and preclude summary judgment. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10786768/radheshvar-llc-v-kenneth-a-perez-larios/

item.title: Giles v. Greenhouse Apartments, LLC (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: The Court of Appeals affirmed summary judgment for an apartment owner and its manager in a negligent-security action by a tenant beaten by unknown assailants on the property in 2020. The landlord conceded it owed the tenant a duty of ordinary care; the affirmance rests solely on causation — the tenant could not establish that any claimed security failure proximately caused the attack — and, given that holding, the court expressly declined to reach the equal-or-superior-knowledge and assumption-of-risk defenses and the challenge to excluded evidence of other crime in the area. Why it matters: Causation is an independently dispositive element of a negligent-security claim: a defendant can win summary judgment without litigating foreseeability at all. The incident predates SB 68, so the common-law framework applies; for incidents on or after April 21, 2025 the analysis runs through the statutory regime at O.C.G.A. §§ 51-3-50 to 51-3-57. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10785227/james-giles-v-greenhouse-apartments-llc/

item.title: Mejia v. SK Battery America, Inc. (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: In a wrongful-death action arising from a fatal fall at a battery-plant construction site, the Court of Appeals affirmed summary judgment for the premises defendants on assumption of the risk, analyzed as an affirmative defense. The decedent, a foreman, had actual knowledge of the specific hazard — twelve days earlier he had watched a coworker fall through the same red-taped, non-weight-bearing louvers — and he stepped onto them without tying off and fell over fifty feet; his repeated safety training and written hazard acknowledgment supplied secondary support for the defense. Why it matters: Actual knowledge drawn from witnessing a prior, identical accident can establish assumption of the risk as a matter of law; documentation like training records and signed acknowledgments corroborates the defense rather than carries it. item.title: Venetian Hills Apartments, LLC v. Hughes (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: In a wrongful-death action after a tenant died in a fire set during an assault by another tenant's guest, the Court of Appeals held the landlord was not entitled to judgment notwithstanding the verdict: it could be liable under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-14 for defective construction and missing fire-safety measures even after parting with possession, and the criminal acts did not demand a defense verdict. The court nonetheless vacated the judgment and ordered a full retrial because the jury charges conflated landlord-tenant and premises-liability law. Why it matters: A landlord can remain liable under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-14 for defective construction and missing fire-safety measures even after giving up possession, but jury charges that blend § 44-7-14 with § 51-3-1 premises law can require a full retrial. item.title: Williams v. Reddick (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: The Court of Appeals reversed summary judgment for a defendant driver in a tractor-trailer collision case. The plaintiff had signed a limited liability release under O.C.G.A. § 33-24-41.1 that preserved claims to the extent other insurance was available, and a fact question remained on whether the employer's policy provided uninsured-motorist coverage, because an undated coverage summary did not establish a valid written rejection under O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(a)(3). Why it matters: A limited liability release under O.C.G.A. § 33-24-41.1 does not end the case where other coverage may exist, and a written uninsured-motorist rejection under O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(a)(3) must actually appear in the record to be effective. item.title: SMG Construction Services, LLC v. Cook (Ga.)
item.description: The Supreme Court of Georgia vacated a Court of Appeals decision that had reversed summary judgment for a property owner whose independent contractor fell from an exposed second-story ledge. The Court held the Court of Appeals conflated actual and constructive knowledge and wrongly used constructive-knowledge principles to create a fact question about the contractor's actual knowledge of the open, unguarded ledge. Because the lower court stopped there, it had not addressed all elements of the owner's defenses, so the case was remanded. Why it matters: Actual knowledge of an open and obvious hazard is analyzed on its own terms under O.C.G.A. § 51-3-1 and is not blurred into the constructive-knowledge inquiry; this is the decision the Mejia panel applied. item.title: Ferriero v. Progressive Premier Insurance Co. (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: The Court of Appeals vacated the dismissal of a collision suit for failure to serve the defendant. The plaintiff had served Progressive as her uninsured-motorist carrier and pointed to a process server's affidavit and email showing copies left with the defendant's mother, and the trial court abused its discretion in finding no evidence of substitute service under O.C.G.A. § 9-11-4(e)(7) when that evidence was in the record. Why it matters: Substitute-service proof under O.C.G.A. § 9-11-4(e)(7) that is in the record must be addressed before dismissing for lack of service, and once the limitation period has run the case turns on the plaintiff's diligence in perfecting service. item.description: The Court of Appeals reversed the denial of partial summary judgment to a John Doe defendant, litigated in the name of the homeowners' uninsured-motorist carrier, after a phantom vehicle allegedly forced another driver into the plaintiffs' house. item.title: Walmart Stores East, LP v. Leverette (Ga.)
item.description: The Supreme Court of Georgia vacated a $1 million "nominal damages" award in a premises injury case in which a shopper was struck by a heavy box. The Court held that nominal damages under Georgia law remain only a trivial sum, as at common law, and overruled the Court of Appeals precedent treating nominal damages as having no maximum. Because a million dollars is not a trivial sum, the judgment was vacated, with the remedy and invited-error questions left for the courts below. Why it matters: Nominal damages under Georgia law remain only a trivial sum, and the Court overruled precedent that had treated them as having no ceiling, so a seven-figure 'nominal' award cannot stand. item.title: Patterson v. United Services Automobile Association (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: The Court of Appeals affirmed the denial of uninsured-motorist coverage to an insured who was struck as a pedestrian and sought UM benefits from USAA. The policy required prompt notice as a condition precedent, and a twenty-one-month delay in notifying the insurer failed that requirement as a matter of law, with the insured's unawareness that UM coverage might apply not excusing the delay. Why it matters: A prompt-notice condition precedent in a first-party uninsured-motorist policy can be enforced as a matter of law, and a long, unexplained reporting delay, here twenty-one months, can forfeit coverage even if the insured did not realize UM might apply. item.title: Docs of CT, LLC v. Biotek Services, LLC (Ga.)
item.description: A party sought to vacate an arbitration award under OCGA section 9-9-13 (b), arguing that ex parte communications between the arbitrator and opposing counsel were per se prejudicial. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that to establish that its rights were prejudiced by one of the listed grounds for vacatur, the moving party must show that the challenged conduct affected or influenced the outcome of the arbitration, and that prejudice is not presumed outside rare contexts. Because the moving party offered no basis for concluding the ex parte communications affected the outcome, the Court affirmed. Why it matters: This decision establishes that prejudice under OCGA section 9-9-13 (b) requires an outcome-focused showing of actual prejudice, so parties seeking to vacate arbitral awards must demonstrate how the challenged conduct affected the result rather than relying on per se or presumed prejudice. item.title: Merritt Island Woodwerx, LLC v. Space Coast Credit Union (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: A credit union moved to compel arbitration under the Federal Arbitration Act after the AAA declined to administer a consumer's demand because the credit union had not registered its arbitration clause or paid the required compliance fee. Applying Bedgood v. Wyndham, the Eleventh Circuit held that the credit union's failure to comply with its chosen arbitral forum's policies placed it in default under Section 3 and rendered relief under Sections 3 and 4 unavailable. The court further held that a co-plaintiff with an identical, already-rejected arbitration clause could rely on a futility showing and need not separately demand arbitration, and that the substitute-forum clause permitted resolution in court because a court is a forum. Why it matters: It establishes that post-filing compliance with arbitral-forum registration requirements cannot cure a party's prior noncompliance that caused the forum to decline arbitration, so a party that delayed remedying a self-created barrier to arbitration cannot later compel it. Also: As to the co-plaintiff that never formally demanded arbitration, the court held that possessing an arbitration provision identical to one the AAA had already refused to administer supplied a sufficient evidentiary basis, in the form of the actual declination letter, to establish futility. That co-plaintiff was therefore not required to make its own arbitration demand before suing, and Section 3 relief was unavailable. Why it matters: It clarifies that a co-plaintiff holding the same already-rejected arbitration clause may rely on a futility showing supported by the prior declination letter rather than making a separate arbitration demand. Also: The court held that under Section 4 of the FAA the credit union could not obtain an order directing arbitration. As to the plaintiff that had attempted to arbitrate, there was no failure, neglect, or refusal to arbitrate; as to the plaintiff that had not demanded arbitration, the credit union was aggrieved by its own noncompliance and the AAA's resulting declination, not by that plaintiff's conduct. Why it matters: It applies Section 4's causal requirement to deny an order compelling arbitration where the movant's own failure to comply with arbitral-forum policies, rather than the opposing party's conduct, caused the inability to arbitrate. item.title: Statham v. Quang (Ga.)
item.description: After a patient was injured during a hysterectomy in which a medical student manipulated a sponge stick under the physicians' supervision, she sought to hold the supervising physicians vicariously liable for the student's negligence. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that OCGA section 51-1-38, which immunizes medical students from civil liability under certain circumstances, neither imposes vicarious liability on supervising physicians nor renders them immune from it, leaving their liability to be determined as otherwise provided by law. The Court further held that a physician may be vicariously liable under respondeat superior for a supervised medical student's negligence where the evidence shows the physician assumed actual control over the student's physical conduct, even absent a contractual right of control, and that the undisputed evidence here created a jury question on that issue. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that a contract disclaiming an agency relationship is not dispositive of vicarious liability and that assumed control over an agent's physical conduct can independently establish a master-servant relationship for respondeat superior, an issue central to medical malpractice and agency law. Also: The Court held that the borrowed servant doctrine operates only as a defense to a respondeat superior claim, relieving a general master of liability when a special master had the right of control, and not as an independent basis for imposing vicarious liability on a defendant. A plaintiff seeking to hold a special master liable for a borrowed servant's conduct must establish the elements of respondeat superior rather than rely on the borrowed servant doctrine itself. The Court disapproved any reading of Hendley v. Evans to the contrary. Why it matters: This resolves how the borrowed servant doctrine functions, confining it to a defensive role and requiring plaintiffs to proceed under respondeat superior to impose vicarious liability. item.title: Prime Property and Casualty Insurance Company v. Kepali Group, Inc. (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: Applying Florida law in a diversity action, the Eleventh Circuit held that a commercial automobile policy's after-acquired auto provision provided continuing coverage for a newly acquired vehicle once the insured gave the required notice within 30 days, because that provision listed only two conditions for coverage and did not make payment of an additional premium a condition precedent. The court rejected the insurer's argument that coverage expired at the end of the 30-day notice period for nonpayment, reasoning that nothing in the provision so stated and that the policy's integration clause barred reliance on extrinsic terms. The court further held that the policy's premium audit and cancellation provisions, not a common-law reasonable-time default, governed when any additional premium was due and how coverage could be terminated for nonpayment, and that the insurer's failure to perform a premium audit or follow the cancellation procedures left coverage in force. The court affirmed the district court's ruling that the insurer had a duty to defend. Why it matters: It clarifies that under Florida law a commercial fleet policy's after-acquired auto provision triggers continuing coverage upon timely notice without requiring premium payment as a condition precedent, and that the policy's own premium audit and cancellation mechanisms control the timing and consequences of nonpayment. item.title: Kinsale Insurance Company v. Pride of St. Lucie Lodge 1189, Inc. (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: Applying Florida law in a diversity action, the Eleventh Circuit reversed summary judgment for the insurer on a common-law bad-faith claim premised on the insurer's failure to initiate settlement negotiations before suit was filed. The court held that, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the nonmovants, a jury could reasonably find that liability was clear under the Powell rule on a negligent-security fact pattern where a bar's security simultaneously ejected two feuding groups into a dark, unmonitored parking lot and a fatal shooting followed within ten to fifteen minutes, with injuries far exceeding the policy sublimit. The court clarified that the Powell 'clear liability' standard is one part of the totality-of-the-circumstances analysis rather than a separate threshold to bad-faith liability, and that 'clear' liability means liability that is obvious or easily understood, not liability that is guaranteed. Why it matters: It clarifies that the duty to initiate settlement negotiations where liability is clear is a component of the totality-of-the-circumstances bad-faith analysis rather than a separate threshold, and defines what 'clear' liability means, guidance relevant to practitioners handling insurer bad-faith and negligent-security matters under analogous frameworks. item.title: Fu Wu v. Chun Liu (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: A defendant removed a state-court action under 9 U.S.C. section 205 of the Federal Arbitration Act, invoking the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards, and moved to compel arbitration. In a single order, the district court denied the motion to compel and remanded for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, finding the defendant could not enforce the arbitration clause. The Eleventh Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. section 1447(d) bars appellate review of such an order because FAA section 16(a)(1)(C) contains no express statutory exception to the remand bar, and neither the matter-of-substantive-law exception nor the Waco exception applies when the arbitration ruling is intrinsic to the jurisdictional determination. The court reasoned that the denial of arbitration was a jurisdictional finding with no conclusive effect on the state action, leaving the state court free to revisit it. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that a litigant cannot use the FAA's appeal-of-arbitration-denial provision to circumvent the section 1447(d) bar when the district court's arbitration ruling is bound up in a jurisdictional remand, defining the limits of appellate review of arbitration-based removal. item.title: Various Insurers, Reinsurers and Retrocessionaires v. General Electric International, Inc. (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: Insurers, suing as subrogees of a power plant owner after a turbine failure, resisted arbitration of claims against various General Electric entities under a services contract their subrogor never signed. Applying federal common law and Section 302 of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, the Eleventh Circuit held that the non-signatory plant owner was an intended third-party beneficiary of the services contract because the contract repeatedly named it as project owner and gave it explicit, unilateral rights, including the right to direct changes to the power train sets and to act in emergencies. As subrogees, the insurers stood in the owner's shoes and were therefore bound by the contract's arbitration clause. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that under federal common law a non-signatory may be compelled to arbitrate as a third-party beneficiary when the contract names it and confers specific enforceable rights, and that a subrogee takes that obligation along with the subrogor's rights. Also: The court separately addressed who decides arbitrability of the individual claims. It held that the services contract's incorporation of the International Chamber of Commerce Conciliation and Arbitration Rules, whose Article 6(4) empowers the arbitral body to decide whether arbitration shall proceed, clearly and unmistakably delegates questions of arbitrability to the arbitrator, extending the reasoning of Terminix from AAA rules to ICC rules. Why it matters: The holding establishes that incorporating ICC arbitration rules, like incorporating AAA rules, delegates the gateway question of arbitrability to the arbitrator rather than the court. item.title: Liberty Surplus Insurance Corporation v. Kaufman Lynn Construction, Inc. (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: Applying Florida law, the Eleventh Circuit construed a Course of Construction Exclusion in a commercial general liability policy, which barred coverage for property damage to any insured project during the course of construction until the project is completed. The court held that the undefined phrase until the project is completed unambiguously means the entire multi-phase project must be finished, not merely the portion that sustained damage, so water damage to completed buildings was excluded while other buildings remained under construction and old buildings remained to be demolished. The court declined to import the policy's products-completed operations hazard definition of completed work into the exclusion, reasoning that your work and project are not synonymous. The coverage ruling was affirmed. Why it matters: It establishes how courts applying Florida law read a Course of Construction Exclusion in a CGL policy, holding that completion of the project means the entire project rather than the damaged component. Also: The court held that an insured has Article III standing to pursue a reformation counterclaim based on mutual mistake even without a pending claim on the disputed portion of the policy. Assuming the reformation claim would succeed, the insured received a policy different from the one it bargained for and paid a premium not commensurate with the coverage provided, which is a concrete and particularized benefit-of-the-bargain economic injury, and the claim presents no ripeness problem because it rests on a past mutual mistake rather than contingent future events. The court reversed the dismissal of the reformation counterclaim and remanded. Why it matters: It clarifies that a reformation claim for an insurance policy may proceed in federal court before any claim is made on the disputed coverage, treating the discrepancy between the bargained-for and issued policy as a present injury. Also: The court held that the insurer could not recover attorney's fees under Florida's offer-of-judgment statute, section 768.79, and Rule 1.442 because its settlement proposal failed to resolve all claims between the parties. By treating the insured's declaratory and breach-of-contract counterclaims as essentially monetary while omitting from the proposal its own mirror-image declaratory-judgment claim regarding coverage, the insurer failed to comply with the requirement that a proposal resolve all claims for monetary relief. The denial of fees was affirmed. Why it matters: It clarifies that under section 768.79 and Rule 1.442 a settlement proposal must resolve all claims between the parties, so a proponent that characterizes the opponent's declaratory claim as monetary cannot omit its own mirror-image declaratory claim from the proposal. item.title: Love v. McKnight (Ga.)
item.description: Plaintiff sought expenses of litigation under OCGA section 13-6-11 based on bad faith after a rear-end collision in which defendant was cited and pleaded guilty to following too closely. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that bad faith under the statute requires conduct that is intentional, wanton, reckless, or at least indicative of conscious indifference to known harmful consequences, and that mere negligence does not suffice. The court held that the violation of a strict-liability traffic law, by itself, does not establish bad faith, and that evidence of distraction from cell phone use, raising at most an issue of negligence, was insufficient to submit the claim to the jury. The court reasoned that allowing litigation expenses in routine negligence cases would contradict the statute's prefatory language that expenses generally shall not be allowed. Why it matters: This decision clarifies that bad faith under OCGA section 13-6-11 requires more than negligence or a traffic-law violation, setting the threshold for submitting litigation-expense claims to a jury in tort and auto cases. item.title: Waetzig v. Halliburton Energy Services, Inc. (U.S.)
item.category: Supreme Court of the United States
item.description: A plaintiff voluntarily dismissed his federal lawsuit without prejudice under Rule 41(a) and submitted his claims to arbitration, then sought to reopen the dismissed case under Rule 60(b) after losing at arbitration. The Supreme Court unanimously held that a Rule 41(a) voluntary dismissal without prejudice qualifies as a "final proceeding" under Rule 60(b), so a district court may use Rule 60(b) to reopen such a case. The Court rejected importing the appellate-jurisdiction concept of finality from 28 U.S.C. section 1291 into Rule 60(b), and read "judgment, order, or proceeding" as ascending in generality so that "proceeding" reaches all steps in an action. The Court expressly declined to decide whether the district court had jurisdiction over the motion to vacate the arbitration award, leaving that and the propriety of relief for remand. Why it matters: It clarifies that a Rule 41(a) voluntary dismissal without prejudice is reachable under Rule 60(b), establishing the mechanism by which a litigant may ask a federal court to reopen a case that was voluntarily dismissed. item.title: Wilson v. Hearos, LLC (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: A plaintiff sued an earplug manufacturer in Georgia state court for product-related hearing loss, and a non-party parent company removed the case to federal court. The Eleventh Circuit held that removal by a non-party, which lacks statutory authority under 28 U.S.C. section 1441(a) to remove, is a waivable procedural defect under 28 U.S.C. section 1447(c) rather than a jurisdictional one, so long as the federal court would have had original subject matter jurisdiction had the case been filed there. Because complete diversity and the amount in controversy were satisfied and the plaintiff did not move to remand within 30 days, the objection was waived. Why it matters: It establishes that a non-party's improper removal does not defeat subject matter jurisdiction and must be challenged within 28 U.S.C. section 1447(c)'s 30-day window or be waived, clarifying when a removal defect can be raised. Also: After removal, the plaintiff argued that Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(m)'s 90-day service window displaced Georgia's service-and-diligence rule for statute-of-limitations purposes. The court held that Georgia's requirement, that service relate back to the filing date only if the plaintiff exercised diligence in perfecting service, is an integral part of the state statute of limitations and is therefore substantive law that continues to apply in federal court under Erie. Rule 4(m) sets only a procedural maximum time to serve and does not extend a state-defined limitations period, so the district court correctly applied Georgia's diligence standard to find the claims time barred. Why it matters: It confirms that Georgia's service-and-diligence tolling rule remains controlling after removal to federal court and is not displaced by Federal Rule 4(m), affecting how limitations defenses are litigated in diversity cases originating in Georgia. item.title: Wasserman v. Franklin County (Ga.)
item.description: Plaintiff sought to assert a third party's federal equal protection rights in Georgia courts under the federal doctrine of third-party standing. The Georgia Supreme Court held that the federal doctrine of third-party standing is not part of Georgia constitutional standing law, because the Judicial Power Paragraph of the Georgia Constitution requires a plaintiff, at a minimum, to assert a violation of her own legal rights to invoke a Georgia court's judicial power, and overruled Burgess and later decisions to the extent they adopted that doctrine. The Court also rejected the plaintiff's Supremacy Clause argument, holding that Georgia's constitutional standing requirement is a neutral jurisdictional rule that may be applied to bar a Section 1983 claim brought by someone asserting only a nonparty's rights. The Court vacated and remanded, leaving the plaintiff's separate assignment-of-claim theory for the courts below to address in the first instance. Why it matters: It establishes that a Georgia plaintiff must assert a violation of her own legal rights to have standing and eliminates federal third-party standing as a basis for suing in Georgia courts, a threshold rule of broad importance to all civil litigators. Also: The plaintiff argued that applying Georgia's standing requirements to bar her federal Section 1983 claim would violate the Supremacy Clause. The Court held that Georgia's constitutional standing rule is a neutral jurisdictional rule that does not target or discriminate against federal causes of action, and so may be applied evenhandedly to bar a Section 1983 claim asserted by a plaintiff who alleges only a nonparty's rights. Why it matters: It clarifies that Georgia's constitutional standing requirement is a neutral jurisdictional rule enforceable against federal claims in state court without offending the Supremacy Clause. item.title: Royal Canin U.S.A., Inc. v. Wullschleger (U.S.)
item.category: Supreme Court of the United States
item.description: Plaintiff sued in state court asserting both federal and state-law claims, and defendant removed based on the federal claim, with the state claims proceeding under supplemental jurisdiction. After removal, plaintiff amended the complaint to delete every federal-law claim and sought remand. A unanimous Court held that when a post-removal amendment excises the federal-law claims that enabled removal, leaving only state-law claims, the federal court loses supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. section 1367 and must remand to state court, because section 1367 draws no distinction between original and removed cases and jurisdiction follows the amended, now operative, pleading. The Court treated the contrary statement in the Rockwell footnote as non-binding dictum that does not withstand analysis. Why it matters: It establishes that a plaintiff who originally pleads federal claims alongside state-law claims can defeat federal jurisdiction after removal by amending to drop all federal claims, requiring remand to state court, which directly bears on removal and remand strategy whenever federal and state tort claims are pleaded together. item.title: Cook-Rose v. Waffle House, Inc. (Ga.)
item.description: Plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed a premises liability suit, filed a renewal action under OCGA section 9-2-61(a), and then sought to appeal a post-dismissal attorneys' fees award entered in the dismissed case by filing a discretionary application. The Court of Appeals dismissed for failure to obtain a certificate of immediate review, reasoning that the pendency of the renewal action meant the case remained pending below. The Supreme Court held that a renewal action is a new case de novo, not a continuance of the dismissed action, so the pendency of the renewal did not keep the dismissed case pending. Because the fee order made the dismissed case no longer pending in the court below, it was a final judgment under OCGA section 5-6-34(a)(1) and no certificate of immediate review was required. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that a post-dismissal attorneys' fees order in a case that has been voluntarily dismissed and renewed is a final judgment appealable by discretionary application without a certificate of immediate review, because the renewal action is a separate new case. item.title: Lubin v. Starbucks Corporation (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: A former employee's spouse, who obtained health coverage as a dependent but never signed an arbitration agreement, brought a putative class action against the employer alleging deficient COBRA notices. The employer moved to compel arbitration under the wife's employment agreement. The Eleventh Circuit held that a non-signatory cannot be compelled to arbitrate under an agreement he did not sign, particularly where his claim arises from an independent federal statutory right rather than from the contract. The court also held that the agreement's delegation clause did not clearly and unmistakably commit arbitrability to the arbitrator because it conflicted with an exclusion clause carving out actions to compel arbitration, so the court, not the arbitrator, decided arbitrability. Why it matters: It clarifies that an arbitration agreement's delegation clause does not provide the clear and unmistakable evidence needed to send arbitrability to the arbitrator when it conflicts with an exclusion clause for actions to compel arbitration, and that a non-signatory suing on an independent statutory right is not bound to arbitrate. Also: The court applied Florida contract law to the employer's three theories for binding a non-signatory. It held that equitable estoppel did not apply because the non-signatory was not relying on or seeking the benefits of the wife's employment agreement, the third-party beneficiary doctrine did not apply because that doctrine binds a beneficiary only when he sues to enforce the contract, and the derivative-claim theory failed because the spouse's right to a COBRA notice under 29 U.S.C. section 1166(a)(4) is an independent statutory right rather than one derivative of the participant's right. Why it matters: It clarifies the limits of the equitable estoppel, third-party beneficiary, and derivative-claim exceptions used to bind non-signatories to arbitration agreements under state contract law. item.title: Whitaker Farms, LLC v. Fitzgerald Fruit Farms, LLC (Ga.)
item.description: After a jury awarded punitive damages on a trespass claim, the defendant challenged the admission of statements its officer made during a settlement conference, which the Court of Appeals had upheld as admissible under OCGA section 24-4-408 (c) to show state of mind. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that a request for punitive damages is a 'claim' within the meaning of Rule 408 (a), and that because a defendant's state of mind is an element of a punitive damages claim, evidence offered to prove that state of mind is offered to prove liability for the claim and is therefore inadmissible. The court did not decide whether Rule 408 (b) categorically excludes all statements made in compromise negotiations. The court vacated and remanded for the Court of Appeals to determine whether the erroneous admission was harmful. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that settlement-conference statements cannot be admitted to prove a defendant's state of mind for purposes of establishing entitlement to punitive damages, because such evidence proves an element of, and thus liability for, the punitive damages claim under OCGA section 24-4-408 (a). item.title: Schleider v. GVDB Operations, LLC (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: Plaintiffs brought state-law survival and wrongful death claims under Florida's Assisted Living Facilities Act, alleging an assisted living facility failed to prevent the spread of COVID-19. item.title: VFS Leasing Co. v. Markel Insurance Company (11th Cir.)

item.title: Gemini Insurance Company v. Zurich American Insurance Company (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit

It directed that interest on the remaining $500,000 run from the date of payment to the date of the amended final judgment. item.title: Titshaw v. Geer (Ga.)
item.description: The Supreme Court of Georgia held that a claim for breach of a contract for legal services may be governed by either the six-year statute of limitation in OCGA section 9-3-24 or the four-year statute in OCGA section 9-3-25, depending on whether the duty allegedly breached arose directly from a written contract, applying the framework set out in Newell Recycling. The Court clarified that the six-year period applies when the breach concerns a duty growing directly out of an enforceable written contract for legal services, including duties implied by law, while the four-year period applies when no written contract exists, the writing is unenforceable, or the breach relates only remotely to the written agreement. The Court disapproved broad readings of Armstrong v. Cuffie and Coe v. Proskauer Rose as suggesting that all breach-of-contract-for-legal-services claims are governed by the four-year period. The judgments were vacated and remanded. Why it matters: The decision establishes that the Newell Recycling framework, not a single fixed limitation period, determines whether the six-year or four-year statute of limitation governs a breach-of-contract-for-legal-services claim. Also: The Court disapproved the Oehlerich/Smiley line of Court of Appeals cases holding that a claim is barred as duplicative of a legal-malpractice claim when it is based on the same conduct, the same damages, and duties from the same source. The Court held that plaintiffs may simultaneously pursue different causes of action with different elements arising from the same underlying conduct, and that a statute of limitation barring one cause of action does not necessarily bar other causes of action based on the same facts, because each claim must be analyzed separately to determine its applicable limitation period and accrual date. Why it matters: The decision confirms that a plaintiff may pursue alternative tort and contract theories arising from the same conduct, and that the timeliness of each claim must be assessed independently rather than treating one claim as duplicative of another. item.title: Jenkins v. BP Exploration & Production Inc. (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: Cleanup workers from the Deepwater Horizon oil spill sued, alleging that exposure to crude oil and dispersants caused chronic sinusitis, and offered toxicology and epidemiology experts on general causation. The Eleventh Circuit held that, under its toxic-tort precedent, a plaintiff must demonstrate the threshold level of exposure that is hazardous to human beings generally as part of general causation, not only specific causation, and that the experts' failure to identify any such harmful dose justified exclusion. The court further held that the experts' opinions were independently excludable for failing to identify a statistically significant association, assess the cited studies' acknowledged limitations, and meaningfully apply the Bradford Hill factors. Applying the abuse-of-discretion standard, the court affirmed the exclusion of both experts and the resulting summary judgment. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that the harmful-dose or threshold-exposure requirement is part of general causation in toxic-tort cases, governing the admissibility of causation experts under Daubert and Rule 702. Also: Independent of the threshold-dose issue, the court held that the experts' opinions were properly excluded because they relied on studies that addressed acute rather than chronic conditions or different diseases, ignored the studies' acknowledged limitations and biases, and offered only a cursory and superficial application of the Bradford Hill factors. The court emphasized that these rulings tested the reliability of the experts' methodology, not the correctness of their conclusions. Why it matters: It reinforces that a toxic-tort general-causation expert must reliably assess study limitations, statistical significance, dose-response, background risk, and the Bradford Hill factors, and that conclusory treatment of those steps supports exclusion. item.title: Steines v. Westgate Palace, L.L.C. (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: Servicemember borrowers brought a class action alleging that a timeshare lender violated the Military Lending Act, and the lender moved to compel arbitration under a delegation clause and the FAA. The Eleventh Circuit held that the antecedent question of whether another act of Congress overrides the FAA always belongs to the court and cannot be delegated to an arbitrator, even by a delegation clause, because the FAA's severability principle applies only if the contract falls within the FAA's scope. The court further held that the MLA, through 10 U.S.C. section 987(e)(3) and (f)(4), unambiguously displaces the FAA and renders any agreement to arbitrate, including a delegation clause, unenforceable against covered servicemembers. Why it matters: It establishes that a challenge to the applicability of the FAA itself, premised on a conflicting federal statute, is a gateway question reserved for the court regardless of a delegation clause, clarifying the limits of delegation agreements in FAA arbitration practice. Also: The court held that the timeshare loan was not within the MLA's exception for a residential mortgage because the floating-week interest in an eighteen-story, 200-unit resort tower is not an interest in a dwelling and is not residential in nature. Applying the persuasive reasoning of its Fair Housing Act precedent, the court found the units function as transient hotel lodging rather than homes. Why it matters: It clarifies how the MLA's residential mortgage exception applies to timeshare financing, treating such interests as transient lodging rather than dwellings. Also: The court held that because the MLA overrides FAA section 2, the remaining FAA provisions, including section 16's interlocutory appeal provision, do not apply, leaving the court without appellate jurisdiction over the appeal from the order denying the motion to compel arbitration. It accordingly dismissed the appeal. Why it matters: It establishes that when a federal statute displaces FAA section 2, FAA section 16 provides no basis for interlocutory appellate jurisdiction over an order denying arbitration. item.description: A named plaintiff sought to certify a class of patients whose protected health information was disclosed by a former facility employee, and the trial court denied certification for lack of commonality and typicality. item.title: ECB USA, Inc. v. Chubb Insurance Company of New Jersey (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: An accounting firm's professional liability policy covered liability arising from management consulting services, defined as services directed toward expertise in banking finance, accounting, risk and systems analysis, design and implementation, asset recovery and strategy planning for financial institutions. Applying New Jersey law and the series-qualifier canon, the court held that the postpositive phrase 'for financial institutions' modifies every parallel item in the list, including 'accounting,' so an audit performed for a non-financial-institution client was not covered. The court rejected the assignees' reliance on the last-antecedent and nearest-reasonable-referent canons, reasoning those canons do not apply to a parallel series of nouns. Second, even if there were a genuine interpretive dispute, contra proferentem does not apply where both parties are sophisticated commercial entities with equal bargaining power, and the insured accounting firm qualified as such.
